1st; I'm not saying it's the best tech - I'm implying that the thing was hobby-shopped. Like a lot of things done in the home lab it COULD have been done better. They creator just didn't know how. Or maybe this was version 0.9 or something in 1997.

3rd; You're right, but just because that's when the ARTICLE was written doesn't mean it was CREATED then. At best, that's just when the Foundation found it.

4th; Ah - gotcha. I was thinking it was was "Send a command, trigger a download." (because, after all HTML files are text, etc).

5th; "Gears' Razor: When in doubt, the scarier option is probably correct."

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
1st; I still think that can be rephrased to something better. Your computer is perfectly capable of an internet connection, yet it does not have a T3 NIC. Hence "…moved to any computer having an appropriate network interface" may be a better phrase.
2nd; OK, point taken.
3rd; 44 megabits? Oh come on, the article was wrtitten 3 years ago. Gigabit ethernet came into being at least 8 years ago.
4th; I object. This thing operates at OSI level 3. The NIC at the computer it is connected to operates at OSI level 3. Files belong to level 7. So, unless some serious SCP magic is happening at the computer, files are not what you should see. Also, in case of Linux-based network equipment you can telnet / ssh to them and change the configuration in-place, via files or commands, but you don't see the files right after you connect your PC to it.
5th; Maybe. The latter makes the whole thing creepier.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
C'mon Gene!

1st; I suspect that was deliberate so it could be powered and not on the internet.

2nd; it's things soldered together that shouldn't be, yet they somehow work. Call it a prototype, because it most certainly is.

3rd; when the article was written it was immense - and for a single device it's still an immense amount of traffic.

4th; yes, seriously. Normal text files are the ways that I get info out of the network routers/switches we use (I'm I.T.). It's also what MANY all the configuration files are in operating systems - Unix or Windows. They're common and universal. Also, we still use serial cables to configure them (which is why Cisco still ships with them); FTP/HTTP is the way you transfer things, not WHAT you transfer and there's no reason to make this too useful.

5th; maybe it doesn't. Maybe it's by mass/volume. Maybe it's looking at things IT finds interesting…

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The latest "Visions of a better world" brought this object to my attention.
Containment procedures: "having a network interface" does not equal "internet access".
Second, what is the last time you've seen a T3 NIC suited for home PCs? Everything I managed to find is a Cisco specialized card for Cisco hardware.
Third, T3 operates at 44 megabits per second. I don't know what medieval hardware would consider this speed "immense".
Fourth. A text file? Seriously? This is a network device, not a disk drive. Maybe a file share, HTTP or FTP server with these files.
Fifth. How does it discern between 17 billions of different bacteria, 33 cockroaches, 4 people and a cactus in the room (see Drewbear's post earlier)?

That said, the idea is good, but the execution is flawed.
